title: The Association Between Skeletal Muscle Mass and Surgical Site Infection, Prognosis in Patients Undergoing Free Flap Reconstructive Surgery for Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma: A Single-Center Retrospective Study
content: Factors influencing oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) prognosis include local and systemic factors, such as nutritional status. Skeletal muscle mass (SMM) loss is a poor prognostic factor not only in elderly patients, but also in cancer patients. We investigated SMM index (SMI), surgical site infection (SSI), and prognosis of patients who underwent resection and free flap reconstructive surgery (FFRS). Ninety-two patients (59 males and 33 females) underwent FFRS between 2013 and 2021. SMM at L3 was measured using preoperative computed tomography. The optimal cutoff for SMM was 49.29 cm2/m2 in males (AUC 0.639) and 41.08 cm2/m2 in females for overall survival (OS) (AUC 0.535). Patients were classified into low and high SMI groups and OS was statistically evaluated. Sixty-three (68.5%) and 29 (31.5 %) patients had low and high SMI, respectively. SSI occurred in 11 (12.0%) patients, and wound dehiscence and delayed wound healing were observed in 22 (23.9%). SSI showed no significant difference between low- and high-SMI groups. In contrast, OS showed significance by age, pathological N (pN), extra nodal extension (ENE), and SMI (high of 89.7%, low of 61.8%). Univariate analyses demonstrated significant associations between OS and age (≥65 vs. &lt;65), SMI (low vs. high), pN (present vs. none), ENE (present vs. none), and albumin (&lt;4.0 vs. ≥4.0). Cox multivariate analysis included SMI (low vs. high; HR: 5.898, 95% CI: 1.691-20.565; P=0.005) and ENE (present vs. none; HR: 9.843, 95% CI: 3.781-25.629; P&lt;0.001). SMI and ENE were independent predictive factors of OS in patients undergoing FFRS for OSCC.
